title: What actually happened when our blog went AI-first: A manager's account
content:
When our blog team made the switch to an AI-first writing model in June 2025, my reaction was split. There was excitement on one side: I could see the inefficiencies in our process that AI might actually fix. On the other, anxiety. And while plenty of that anxiety was about the technology itself (how well these tools could actually write, how much we could trust them), my primary concern was my team.
I’ve managed HubSpot’s blog writing team for three years, and before that was a HubSpot Blog writer myself. I understand what it means to have ownership over your process. Many of the writers I manage got into this work because they love writing. They enjoy the craft of finding the right sentence and earning a reader’s attention. Traffic numbers and conversions are secondary. During this AI transition, I felt the weight of what it could mean for those whose entire approach to their craft was changing fast.
So much of the public conversation about AI content gets the story wrong. There’s an assumption that because AI can write passably well, the hard part is over. Just apply the same low-effort polish you’d apply to an AI-drafted email or memo to your blog post, then ship it.
But I can tell you from experience: it doesn’t work that way. A blog post is meant to compete against dozens (or hundreds) of other posts on the same topic. In this game, generic, low-effort writing will not win, and that’s good news for your content team. It means that even though the writing process has changed, the craft remains important.
So, how do you balance craftsmanship with the efficiency gains AI promises? And how do you build a process that takes advantage of what AI is actually good at without falling into its traps? We spent the last year figuring that out. Here, I’ll share what we learned: where time was saved, where it got added, and what it takes to make AI work without compromising the quality standards you’ve spent years building.
Before AI, our writing process was, well, a writing process. While we had editorial standards and guardrails to ensure consistent quality, we didn’t enforce a specific method for how posts should be written. We hired writers and editors for their ability to craft, and we trusted them to use that ability. We understood that writing is more than just a technical skill. Giving our writers the space to develop their own individual workflows yielded content with personality and unique insights.
When training new writers, we taught a simple, flexible framework to help folks start to structure their time:
For a standard blog post, you’re easily looking at a full day’s work, usually longer. The bulk of that time lived in the drafting phase — writing the words, finding the right structure, and figuring out how to explain something clearly was the core of the job.
When we formally adopted AI-assisted writing in June 2025, my approach was deliberate: don’t over-prescribe. Allowing our writers to develop their own processes had served us well for over a decade, and we wanted to maintain that sense of control for our writing team as much as possible, even as we added AI to the mix.
We gave writers access to AI tools (specifically Claude and ChatGPT , along with NotebookLM) and space to figure out how to work them into their process. Even with AI, I believed writing is personal, and I wasn’t going to tell a team of experienced writers exactly how to do their jobs. Our goal was experimentation first, structure later.
What followed was not the clean efficiency win I expected. AI solved some problems and introduced new ones. But by working through those problems with our writers, we built a process that we know works.
At first, the signs were good. Writers were putting words on the page faster than before, and I assumed that would translate directly into faster posts overall.
A couple of months in, after reviewing time tracking data and having conversations with my team, a more complicated picture emerged. The quantity of posts stayed about the same, but posts were getting longer, more detailed, and more demanding to produce. Writers were spending more time testing software, sourcing expert quotes, reviewing tools in-depth, and going deeper on topics. The time AI saved in drafting was being absorbed by everything else a competitive post requires.
What made it harder was that some writers felt the pressure of both expectations at once: write faster and write more. When I understood that this was happening, I had to recalibrate. AI hadn’t decreased the workload. In many ways, it had increased the workload.
So my first lesson was: If you’re measuring AI’s impact on your team purely by post count, you’re going to be disappointed. The win is in what those posts become, not how fast they get there.
I also assumed AI would make research faster. After all, instead of spending an hour getting up to speed on a topic, a writer could ask Claude and move on.
For general topic knowledge, that’s actually true. On well-documented subjects with plenty of training data to draw from, AI can explain concepts clearly, answer follow-up questions, and get a writer up to speed faster than navigating a dozen browser tabs.
The shortcomings, however, were flagged by writers almost immediately.
The first time it really surfaced was on a listicle covering competitor products. A writer came back to me flagging that the pricing information AI had surfaced was wrong. Not slightly off, but fully outdated. AI didn’t know the pricing had changed, and it didn’t flag its own uncertainty.
I probably should have seen that one coming. After all, a tool trained on data from months ago obviously can’t know that a competitor changed their pricing. But it took a writer caring enough to flag it before I accounted for it.
From this, we learned that for anything requiring accuracy about competitor pricing or features, AI research falls apart. This makes sense when you think about how these tools work: An LLM’s training data has a cutoff date, meaning it’s unlikely to reflect the latest pricing changes, feature updates, or product rebranding. And when AI tools do attempt a live web search, they’re only as good as the pages they can parse. Product pages are often structured in ways that are difficult for an LLM to interpret, which makes even real-time lookups prone to inaccuracies. The result is information that sounds authoritative but may be months or years out of date.
We produce a lot of competitor listicles and product-focused content, and for those, research still requires significant manual effort. So while AI has sped up general-topic research, competitor- and product-focused research takes roughly the same amount of time as it always has.
The research problem ran much deeper than product pricing alone. Beyond outdated competitor data, we were seeing fabricated statistics, misattributed quotes, and incorrect terminology, all delivered with the same confident, authoritative tone. AI doesn’t know what it doesn’t know.
We place a high premium on accuracy, and these so-called AI hallucinations turned fact-checking from a light final step into one of the most time-consuming parts of the process. In some cases, AI drafting took longer than manual drafting because writers had to spend time verifying what the AI got wrong.
What struck me was how quickly my team caught it. That commitment to publishing only truthful, verified information is exactly what separates a good writer from a content generator. It reinforced something I already believed: the writer matters more than the tools they use.
To address hallucinations, we introduced a new formal step in our process: dedicated fact-checking. Pre-AI, writers were responsible for the accuracy of their own research, and a final editorial pass would catch anything obvious. With AI in the mix, fact-checking became its own distinct phase. For a typical post, I estimate it adds around 30 to 60 minutes to the process. It’s longer for research-heavy pieces or anything involving stats, quotes, or product information.
Sure, you could skip fact-checking and assume AI gets everything right. But is that really the standard you want to hold your content to? Publishing misinformation, even unintentionally, damages trust in a way that’s hard to recover from.
QA time grew too, for reasons beyond what fact-checking was already catching. Fact-checking is the process of verifying that the information in a post is correct. QA is about everything else: Does this post sound like a person wrote it? Does it meet our editorial standards? Is it structured in a way that search engines and AI tools can parse?
Without a structured quality layer, AI-assisted drafts introduced problems writers wouldn’t necessarily catch on their own, such as:
To address this, I built a custom QA checker directly into Google Docs that flags these problems and more. It’s become a required step in our workflow.
Through all the changes above, some things didn’t move. The E-E-A-T requirements we had before AI — original quotes, firsthand perspectives, solid data sourcing — stayed intact. Editorial judgment stayed intact. The strategic thinking that goes into deciding what a post needs to say, and who it needs to say it to, stayed intact.
AI handles much of the execution now: drafting, scoping, generating topic angles, and explaining concepts. But the layer of work that makes a piece worth reading (the human perspective, the original insight, the rigorous sourcing) is still on the writer. If anything, it matters more now because it’s what separates your content from everyone else’s AI output.
To understand what changed, it helps to see it. Here’s a rough breakdown of how time was distributed across a typical blog post before AI, and how that distribution shifted after we adopted it:
Note: Time estimates are averages based on HubSpot Blog Team internal tracking. Individual posts vary based on topic complexity, length, and content type.
Of course, the reality varies more than these charts suggest. A writer might draft for an hour, realize they need more research, go back to drafting, catch something that needs fact-checking, and return to drafting again. A real workflow looks more like this:
If AI can generate a blog post in minutes, why not just publish and move on? More content means more chances to rank, more surface area for leads, and more output for less effort, right?
Early in the AI content boom, we all noticed a certain strategy emerging in the SEO space: Publish as much AI-generated content as possible, as fast as possible, and capture market share before competitors caught on. Flood the zone. It operates on the belief that volume alone would be enough to win.
The content that comes from such a fast-and-loose strategy is recognizable to anyone who’s spent time in this industry.
A blog post that strings together sentences without saying much. A listicle that could have been written about any company in any industry. No original data. No real point of view. No specific examples that couldn’t have been fabricated. And if you run it through a plagiarism checker, you’ll even find content that was lifted from competing sources (not intentionally, but as a byproduct of how LLMs work).
In short, it’s generic. You’ve probably heard the term “AI slop” to describe this kind of content as well. Experienced readers and, more importantly, search algorithms can spot slop from a mile away, and it hurts far more than it helps.
Marketers are catching on. According to HubSpot’s 2026 State of Marketing Report , 52% of marketers believe AI has made content so easy to create that it’s become less effective overall.
Need more proof? In 2026, SEO expert Lily Ray tracked more than 220 websites that identified themselves as customers of AI content creation platforms and found a consistent pattern: rapid growth in organic traffic, followed by a steep decline that, in many cases, erased the gains entirely. Across her dataset, more than half of the sites lost at least 30% of their peak organic traffic, and nearly a quarter lost 75% or more.
Here’s an example of what that looks like for one such website.
I understand why teams took to this approach at first. The pressure to produce is real: 83% of marketers say they’re expected to create more content than ever because of AI .
But this is exactly what leading only with speed looks like in practice. If quality becomes something you try to retrofit after the fact, it rarely works.
The teams doing AI writing well start from the opposite end. They define what “good” looks like — voice, depth, accuracy, originality — and then work backward to determine where AI can help them get there faster without compromising on those standards. All writing is anchored in quality from the beginning.
On the HubSpot Blog, that means keeping our E-E-A-T requirements intact. We build quality guardrails into our workflow and are honest about which content types benefit from AI involvement and which don’t. For example, a how-to guide and a piece of original research will have different requirements, and treating them the same way will result in generic content that goes unnoticed.
As former Director of the HubSpot Blog Karla Hesterberg puts it: “The only truly effortless process produces slop.” Teams that resist the slop, keep good writers in the driver’s seat, and use AI as a lever rather than a replacement are the ones producing work that converts.
For a more thorough dive into how we maintain quality standards in an AI-assisted editorial process, check out this post from HubSpot Blog writer Amy Rigby on how HubSpot creates quality content in the age of AI .
Almost overnight, my role shifted in two directions at once. On one side, I became more process-oriented than I’d ever been. I had to think more deeply about workflows, tooling, and how posts get assembled. On the other, people management got harder. Not because my writers were difficult, but because I was asking them to change how they work.
Process changes are relatively straightforward to document, but maintaining motivation and morale through a transition that fundamentally changed their jobs is a different problem entirely. You can build the most thoughtful AI writing process in the world, but if your writers aren’t bought in, none of it works.
Writers come to this job for different reasons, and AI lands differently depending on which reason that is.
Some writers are wired for outcomes . They get into content marketing because they’re good at writing and they like seeing the business impact. For them, AI is a welcome change because it gets them to the result more quickly.
Other writers came to this work because they love the craft . The writing process is something they care about deeply. For them, an AI-first model can feel like it’s taking something away. I don’t see this as a performance issue or a failure to adapt. It’s an internal tension that should be taken seriously.
As a manager, my job is to recognize where each team member falls on that spectrum and work with them accordingly. I create a space for honest feedback, including negative feedback about AI. I know that if writers don’t feel comfortable telling me what isn’t working, I’ll build processes on bad information. The writers who most honestly pushed back on our early AI workflows gave me the clearest roadmap for what needed fixing.
Here’s what I’d tell any manager navigating AI writing:
The goal hasn’t changed: a team that produces work worth reading. The path to get there just looks different from what it did in 2024.
A year into this transition, I’m proud of where we landed, even though we’re still figuring some things out.
What made the difference wasn’t only the tools, but the writers. I knew that going in, and this past year confirmed it at every turn. The writers who pushed back honestly gave me the roadmap, and the ones who struggled helped me understand what was actually being asked of them.
What sticks with me most from this experience is something writers have started saying recently: that they’re feeling like real writers again. The balance between AI efficiency and actual craft has started to feel sustainable. That happened not because we found a perfect prompt or the right tool, but because we never let go of what made our content good in the first place.
If you’re an editorial lead navigating the AI shift right now, know this: What gets you through is having writers who care enough to be honest with you, and being a manager who creates space for that honesty. Don’t underestimate what it means for a writer to feel like a writer. It shows up in the work.
AI is a tool. Keep your writers at the center, hold the quality line, and the rest follows.

title: Best Claude skills for marketing and sales teams
content:
The best Claude skills for marketing and sales teams turn recurring work into reusable processes with defined instructions, inputs, and outputs. Claude skills are reusable instruction sets for tasks such as campaign planning, sales call recaps, persona research, content outlining, proposal drafting, and performance reporting. Claude skills save marketers, sales leaders, and revenue teams from rebuilding the same instructions every time a task recurs.
Claude skills enable teams to refine instructions as requirements change, while strategy, factual validation, and business decisions remain under human control. This guide explains which Claude skills are most useful for marketing and sales teams, how to build practical examples, and when authorized HubSpot context can make the work more relevant.
Claude skills are reusable processes that teach Claude how to complete a task using established instructions and resources. A prompt usually guides a single interaction, while a skill preserves a process that Claude can apply across similar requests. Claude skills help marketing and sales teams standardize recurring work without rebuilding instructions each time.
A Claude skill contains reusable instructions for a defined task. Skills can also include templates, reference documents, examples, scripts, or other supporting resources. A practical Claude skill usually defines the following.
Claude’s skill architecture can also include optional scripts, references, and assets alongside the core instructions. These resources give Claude additional material when a particular task requires it.
Claude skills also support developer workflows. A Claude Code skill can package instructions for recurring development tasks, including a Claude Code review skill that applies the same review criteria across code changes.
A Claude skill is a better fit when a task happens regularly and follows an established process. Marketing calendars, call recaps, proposal drafts, and reporting narratives are common examples.
A regular prompt still works well for quick questions and one-off tasks. Skills become more valuable when teams need to preserve business rules, formatting requirements, source material, or validation steps across future requests.
Teams exploring broader Claude use cases can also see how HubSpot used Claude to create a virtual assistant .
The best Claude skills for marketing and sales teams support work that happens frequently, uses identifiable source material, and produces an output that can be checked before anyone acts on it. Campaign planning, sales follow-up, persona research, content outlining, proposal drafting, and performance reporting meet those criteria particularly well.
A Campaign Brief and Calendar Builder converts campaign inputs into a defined planning framework. Campaign managers, content marketers, and demand generation teams supply the goal, audience, offer, channels, dates, and approved messaging, then use the skill to organize that information into a brief, timeline, and asset plan.
The Campaign Brief and Calendar Builder skill flags missing audience definitions, unclear campaign goals, and unresolved deadlines so marketers can address those gaps before drafting continues.
Review focus: Strategy, priorities, deadlines, and ownership.
Marketing Hub gives marketers tools to execute campaigns and monitor performance once the plan is approved. The HubSpot connector for Claude can also support tasks such as checking page performance, creating or updating landing pages, and drafting marketing emails when relevant HubSpot context is available.
A Sales Call Recap and Follow-Up Planner converts meeting context into organized follow-up recommendations. Account executives, SDRs, and sales managers provide call notes, a transcript, and relevant deal information. Claude then returns a recap with action items, unresolved questions, and a draft follow-up.
The skill should distinguish confirmed prospect statements from recommended next steps. Salespeople still need to evaluate how the follow-up reflects the conversation, account relationship, and proposed next action. HubSpot’s guide to sales skills covers the broader communication skills involved.
Prior interactions or deal history can make the recap more relevant. Authorized HubSpot context can provide that history without requiring salespeople to copy individual records into Claude manually.
A Persona and ICP Research Assistant turns approved research into organized audience insights. Product marketers, demand generation teams, and sales leaders supply interview notes, survey findings, approved customer or account research, and other source material to identify pain points, buying triggers, objections, and decision criteria.
The source material defines which conclusions Claude has evidence to support. Instructions can require support for major findings, distinguish recurring themes from isolated observations, and flag gaps that need more research.
Watch for: Weak source material, unsupported inferences, or invented demographic and firmographic characteristics.
Evidence requirements keep the Persona and ICP Research Assistant focused on research synthesis and leave unsupported details unresolved.
A Blog and Social Post Outliner turns a topic, keyword, brief, or approved research into an organized content plan. The skill works especially well when content teams use established editorial requirements across many assignments.
Detailed writing guidance gives Claude clearer boundaries around terminology, tone, and editorial conventions. HubSpot’s guide to training AI to write in a brand voice offers additional guidance for developing those instructions.
Content teams comparing AI writing processes can also read HubSpot’s experiment writing a blog post with ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini .
A Proposal and One-Pager Draft Helper turns approved discovery information into sales collateral drafts. Sales and account teams provide discovery notes, product facts, scope requirements, and an existing template. Claude then has a defined structure for producing the first draft.
Reviewers should apply closer scrutiny to pricing, contractual commitments, product claims, and legal language in proposal drafts. A defined template gives reviewers more time to check whether the proposal accurately reflects the opportunity and approved commercial terms.
Once the proposal structure is approved, the same source material can enable a Claude presentation skill to convert the proposal content into a presentation deck. HubSpot’s guide to presentation skills for marketers covers the human skills involved in shaping that presentation.
A Reporting and Performance Narrative Assistant converts performance metrics into a business summary. Marketing leaders, sales leaders, and revenue operations teams provide approved metrics, targets, reporting periods, and definitions, then use Claude to surface notable changes, anomalies, and questions that deserve further analysis.
A Reporting and Performance Narrative Assistant should separate observable results from explanations that require more evidence. A declining conversion rate, for example, can be reported as a measured change without assigning a cause the available data cannot establish.
A Claude Excel skill supports the analysis when the underlying metrics live in spreadsheets. Authorized HubSpot marketing, sales, or deal information can add business context when the reporting task requires it.
Marketing and sales teams should start with Claude skills that solve frequent, relatively low-risk tasks and produce easy-to-check outputs. Content outlining and campaign planning offer practical entry points for marketers, while sales teams can begin with call recaps before moving into higher-stakes collateral.
Marketing teams can start with a Blog and Social Post Outliner because its inputs are straightforward and the output is easy for an editor to evaluate. A Campaign Brief and Calendar Builder is a logical next step once campaign inputs and planning templates are established. A practical progression is:
This progression moves from drafting support toward tasks that require more business context and interpretation.
Sales teams should start with a Sales Call Recap and Follow-Up Planner because call notes or a transcript provide a clear source for checking the result. A Proposal and One-Pager Draft Helper fits next once approved templates and product language are available. A practical sales starter set includes:
As sales teams expand how they use skills, access to permitted deal and engagement information can reduce the amount of context they must supply manually. The HubSpot connector for Claude supports that next stage for HubSpot users.
Useful Claude skill examples often start with work a team already repeats manually. A strong skill defines the task, identifies the information Claude needs, specifies the output, and explains how to handle missing or unsupported information.
A campaign brief prompt should define the business goal, audience, source material, required sections, and validation constraints. Campaign-specific information can change while the underlying framework stays in place.
Campaign brief prompt: Create a campaign brief using the information provided below.
Source material: [approved research, messaging, or reference files]
Organize the brief into these sections: campaign objective, audience, key message, offer, channel plan, timeline, required assets, and measurement plan. Use only the supplied information for factual claims. Clearly label missing information or assumptions that require review.
Turning the campaign brief prompt into a reusable skill requires a fixed brief structure and mandatory inputs. Approved brand and reference files provide the supporting context. The instructions should also flag missing information and identify decisions about audience, positioning, timing, or channels that marketers need to make.
Marketing Hub supports execution and measurement after the campaign plan is approved.
A sales discovery recap prompt should separate confirmed customer statements from inferred recommendations. The resulting skill preserves that distinction every time it processes discovery notes or transcripts.
Sales discovery recap prompt: Review the supplied discovery call notes or transcript and create a structured recap. Use only information supported by the source material.
Include confirmed needs, relevant customer language, objections, commitments, and open questions. Place proposed follow-up actions in a separate section. Flag details that require human confirmation. Leave pricing, timelines, commitments, and deal status unresolved unless the source explicitly supports them.
Key instruction to preserve in the skill: Separate confirmed conversation details from proposed actions so a salesperson can quickly identify what came from the customer and what Claude is recommending.
Permitted deal and engagement history from HubSpot can support the recap when relevant, reducing the need to copy individual records into the prompt.
A persona research prompt should instruct Claude to synthesize supplied evidence and label unsupported conclusions. The skill organizes research into useful patterns while preserving gaps in the available evidence.
Persona research prompt: Analyze the approved research provided and create a persona summary for [audience segment]. Base every conclusion on the supplied sources.
Organize the findings into observed pain points, buying triggers, objections, decision criteria, and relevant patterns. Cite the supporting source for each major finding when possible. Create an “Unknowns” section for questions the evidence cannot answer, and clearly label conclusions that require additional validation.
Key instruction to preserve in the skill: Treat missing evidence as an unknown and connect major conclusions to supplied research.
Authorized HubSpot information serves as an additional source when existing business context is relevant to the research.
Claude skills define how Claude performs recurring tasks, while the HubSpot connector for Claude gives Claude permission-based access to authorized HubSpot context. The connector brings relevant HubSpot information into Claude, enabling people to analyze business context and take supported actions without manually copying records between tools. HubSpot remains the system where the underlying records live, and existing HubSpot user permissions continue to govern access.
For existing HubSpot users, the connector reduces the need to move between tools when a task requires HubSpot context. Claude-native users can work with permitted contacts, deals, and other business information from the Claude interface while HubSpot remains the record system.
The HubSpot connector for Claude adds business context that a task might otherwise require someone to supply manually. A sales recap, for example, can use permitted deal and engagement records when that history is relevant.
The HubSpot connector for Claude connects authorized HubSpot context to Claude. Claude respects existing HubSpot user permissions, and HubSpot records remain in HubSpot while Claude accesses permitted information. The connector can turn authorized HubSpot context into actionable answers and support next steps inside Claude. A HubSpot-connected process follows four basic steps:
Permission-aware HubSpot use cases include sales preparation, pipeline analysis, follow-up, and record-keeping. Existing HubSpot business information and engagement history provide the context for these tasks. Examples include:
Claude can create and update supported HubSpot records but cannot delete existing records. Proposed deal changes, customer-facing drafts, and other consequential actions need closer scrutiny when business judgment is involved.
The HubSpot connector for Claude is available with an active HubSpot account (including the free edition) and a paid Claude Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise subscription. The connector works through Claude’s web and desktop experiences; mobile is not currently supported. Existing HubSpot permissions continue to govern what information each connected user can access.
Users connect HubSpot to Claude through Claude’s connector directory. The authorization process links the accounts while preserving the permissions associated with the HubSpot user.
After setup, HubSpot can be selected inside Claude when a task requires relevant business information. The underlying records continue to live in HubSpot.
Claude skills best practices include descriptive naming, simple version control, specific brand guidance, appropriate human oversight, and data minimization. These practices make skills easier to maintain as source material and business requirements change.
Claude skill names should clearly describe the task or intended output. Specific names such as “Campaign Brief Builder” make the purpose easier to recognize than broad labels. Clear names help teams identify the right skill quickly as the library grows. A useful formula is: Task + Output or purpose.
Claude skills should use simple version control when instructions, supporting files, or output requirements change. Version records show which process produced an output and make outdated instructions easier to identify.
Versioning becomes especially useful when source material changes. Proposal skills may need new product messaging, while reporting skills may need revised metric definitions.
Claude skills produce more consistent brand content when the instructions include approved terminology, concrete examples, and specific writing behaviors. Broad descriptions such as “friendly” or “professional” give Claude less actionable direction than specific rules Claude can apply to the output.
A shared brand reference can support several content skills. HubSpot’s guide to training AI to write in a brand voice explains how detailed voice characteristics and examples can give AI systems clearer direction.
Teams should focus human review on outputs involving material business judgment, factual claims, customer commitments, customer-facing content, or proposed record actions. Human review improves accuracy and oversight in AI-assisted workflows. Closer review is warranted when an output includes:
Teams should calibrate the level of human scrutiny to reflect the potential consequence of an error. For instance, a content outline usually requires less attention than a proposal that includes pricing or a change to an active deal.
A Claude skill should receive only the information required for its defined task. Data minimization narrows the context Claude needs to process and makes each input easier to evaluate.
Teams should allow task relevance and access permissions to determine what information enters a skill. Teams should reduce the context supplied to each skill to the smallest useful field set, excluding information that does not affect the requested output.
The HubSpot connector for Claude reinforces this permission-aware approach. Claude accesses HubSpot information through the existing permissions associated with the connected user.
Skills in Claude are reusable instructions and resources for recurring tasks. Prompts usually guide individual interactions, while skills preserve a process that Claude can apply again.
The HubSpot connector for Claude lets users connect HubSpot through Claude’s connector directory without custom coding. Users authorize access, and Claude operates within the permissions associated with the connected HubSpot account. HubSpot records remain in HubSpot while Claude accesses permitted business context.
Claude skills turn approved call context into summaries, action items, open questions, and draft follow-up messages. A skill can also distinguish confirmed customer statements from suggested next steps. Salespeople should verify commitments, timing, factual details, and customer-facing language before using the output.
Claude outputs become more consistent when skills include trusted source material, formatting requirements, specific brand guidance, and clear validation criteria. Version control keeps those instructions up to date as business requirements change.
HubSpot’s guide to training AI to write in a brand voice provides additional guidance for defining useful AI writing instructions.
AI-generated content and notes should live in the business system where the related work is managed and authorized team members can evaluate the information. For HubSpot use cases, approved notes, tasks, and supported updates can remain associated with the relevant HubSpot records.
The HubSpot connector for Claude provides access to permitted HubSpot context while HubSpot remains the system where those records live.
The best first Claude skill supports work that happens often, uses clearly defined inputs, and produces an output that is easy to check. Marketing teams often begin with content or campaign planning, while sales teams often start with call recaps and follow-up processes.
Teams should start with one Claude skill to create room for refining the instructions, source material, and validation process before expanding into higher-risk work. The best Claude skills give teams a reusable process for recurring tasks, while human review supplies the judgment needed for consequential decisions.
For HubSpot users, the HubSpot connector for Claude can add authorized business context when a task requires information from HubSpot. Claude provides the working interface, while HubSpot remains the system where the underlying records live.

title: The psychological advantage of incrementality testing
content:
One of the most underrated benefits of incrementality testing is the psychological advantage it gives marketers: the conviction to make changes.
Marketing is a profession where change often feels risky. Cutting spend, shifting budgets, or walking away from a tactic that seems to perform well can feel like putting the business at risk. If sales decline following a budget reduction, marketing will likely face some difficult questions. Marketers don’t relish those questions from finance. But much of that perceived risk stems from a lack of confidence in the actual contribution of marketing to business outcomes.
An incrementality-backed measurement system gives marketers evidence to challenge that perceived risk — and the confidence to act. It also gets marketing and finance speaking the same language: the language of contribution profit.
The world’s most powerful SEO platform, purpose-built for Enterprise.
When you don’t know how much revenue is truly incremental, maintaining the status quo feels like the safer decision. Even when it might cost the business money. There’s an asymmetry here: Marketers often perceive reducing spend as risky while treating continued investment in potentially inefficient tactics as safe. But the status quo isn’t risk-free.
There’s a real cost to maintaining investments that don’t generate sufficient incremental returns. Every dollar allocated to an inefficient tactic is a dollar that could go somewhere more productive or simply return to the business as profit. Yet those costs are often less visible than the potential consequences of making a change. It’s easier to explain why you maintained an existing budget than why you decided to cut one, particularly when the attribution-based performance reporting available to you suggests everything is working.
This is where incrementality testing changes the dynamic. Imagine knowing with reasonable confidence that a particular channel or tactic generates incremental revenue, but at a return that doesn’t justify the investment. Perhaps the platform reports a 4x ROAS, but your testing suggests the true incremental return is closer to 1.5x. At a 40% contribution margin, every dollar invested generates just $0.60 in incremental contribution before media cost. That’s $0.40 of contribution profit lost per dollar spent at the measured return. Suddenly, reducing spend isn’t just a potentially risky move. It’s an opportunity to increase contribution margin dollars.
This doesn’t necessarily mean eliminating the investment altogether. Marketing returns are rarely linear, and a channel that’s unprofitable at its current level of spend might be highly profitable at a lower one. The marginal return matters when determining how aggressively to reduce investment. But understanding the underlying economics gives you a much better starting point for deciding what to change and where to look for additional opportunities.
There’s something freeing about that level of understanding. It shifts the conversation from “What if we hurt the business by making this change?” to “What opportunity are we missing by not making it?” Instead of disproportionately focusing on the downside of changing course, marketers can start evaluating decisions through the lens of potential upside — and upside to contribution profit, a metric that matters to your finance stakeholders a lot more than ROAS.
Without a credible understanding of incrementality, budget conversations can become exercises in defending the existing plan. Teams debate attribution, point to platform-reported performance, and look for reassurance that changing investment levels won’t negatively affect revenue. Even when everyone suspects there are inefficiencies, it can be difficult to muster enough conviction to act on them.
With incrementality evidence, the conversation becomes more productive. Instead of debating whether a channel deserves its existing budget because it reports strong performance, teams can discuss whether the incremental returns justify the investment. They can make decisions based on the business’s economics rather than the optics of a marketing dashboard. That doesn’t make every decision easy, but it creates a much clearer framework for making one.
There’s also a cumulative benefit to this process. The more consistently a team tests, learns, and acts on the results, the more comfortable it becomes challenging existing assumptions. Decisions that once required extensive debate can become relatively straightforward when there’s a shared understanding of how to evaluate them . Over time, incrementality testing becomes more than a measurement capability. It becomes a foundation for faster, more confident decision-making.
This also changes the relationship between marketing, finance, and leadership. Too often, marketing finds itself in the position of defending spend while finance challenges whether that spend is necessary. When marketing reports revenue that may have happened anyway, there’s an inherent disconnect between the performance being celebrated and the financial outcomes the business experiences.
Incrementality testing helps close that gap. It gives both sides a more credible foundation for discussing investment decisions, trade-offs, and profitability. Rather than approaching budget conversations from opposing positions, teams can align around a shared objective: What decisions will create the most incremental profit for the business? Marketing becomes less about justifying its budget and more about helping determine where the business should invest its next dollar.
That alignment also creates an opportunity for marketing to elevate its role within the organization. When marketers can articulate the incremental contribution profit generated by their investments, they participate in the same capital allocation conversations as the rest of the business. The conversation is no longer simply about how much budget marketing needs, but how marketing can help the business achieve its financial objectives.

Incrementality testing doesn’t eliminate uncertainty, nor does it make decisions for you. A test provides evidence about a particular investment under particular conditions, and the economics can change as budgets scale, consumer behavior shifts, or the competitive environment evolves. Knowing a tactic is inefficient doesn’t automatically tell you exactly how much to cut, where to reinvest, or what to test next. That’s still the marketer’s job.
The objective isn’t perfect certainty or outsourcing judgment to a measurement system. It’s about building enough confidence to make better decisions faster while continuing to learn. The real value comes when marketers combine incrementality evidence with business context, strategic judgment, and a willingness to act. Each test creates another opportunity to challenge assumptions, improve the allocation of capital, and build institutional confidence in the process.
This makes marketing a lot more fun. When you understand the economics of your investments, you’re more willing to experiment, challenge conventional wisdom, and pursue opportunities that might otherwise feel too risky. You no longer just manage budgets and defend performance reports. You actively look for ways to make the business more profitable.
When you stack those better-informed decisions over time, the compounding impact on business performance can be significant. Not necessarily because any individual decision is transformative, but because consistently making smarter investment decisions creates value that accumulates.
When you don’t understand incrementality, changing your media mix or strategy feels risky. When you do, not changing it can feel even riskier.
The value of incrementality testing isn’t just knowing what works. It’s having the conviction to act on what you learn.
